title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; implied expectations are what you must beat. Before calling a stock cheap or expensive, ask what return on equity and growth rate the market has already wired into today's quote.
epigraph.author: Valuation Discipline Maxim

web_blocks.html: At the verified November 13, 2026 close of $346.19, JPMorgan Chase commands an ~$921 billion market cap (~$897.84B–$921B across 2.66B shares) [20, 21]. The stock trades at 14.52x trailing TTM P/E ($23.84 TTM EPS) and 2.62x book value ($132.30/sh) [20]. On FY2025 tangible book value ($107.56/sh), it trades at 3.22x P/TBV with a 1.78% trailing dividend yield ($6.15 TTM) [1, 20]. At first glance, 3.22x tangible book looks steep compared to the post-2008 decade, when big banks traded at 1.0x–1.6x TBV. Yet P/TBV without Return on Tangible Common Equity (ROTCE) is incomplete. A bank earning 20% ROTCE and compounding TBVPS at ~8.5%–10.5% annually justifies a ~2.8x–3.3x TBV multiple under Gordon Growth math.

Reverse DCF / Implied Expectations: Assume a 9.5% cost of equity and a 4.0% perpetual nominal growth rate. At 3.22x FY25 P/TBV, the market implies a through-the-cycle ROTCE of ~17.3%–17.7% [4, 21]. That sits right in line with management's 17% through-the-cycle target [4]. In short, Wall Street is not pricing in permanent 20%–22% peak ROTCE. Today's quote already discounts ~250 bps of ROTCE normalization as rates ease and card charge-offs normalize toward ~3.2%. If JPM holds 18.5%–19.5% ROTCE through the cycle while TBVPS compounds toward ~$118–$120 in FY2026–2027, fair value rises toward $388.09 (~3.25x forward TBV / ~16.3x TTM EPS). That offers +12.10% upside from $346.19 plus the ~1.8% dividend.

web_blocks.takeaway: JPMorgan Chase trades at a modest P/E premium to BAC (11.94x), WFC (11.96x), and C (11.84x), and near Morgan Stanley (14.72x), despite superior 20% ROTCE and unmatched scale.

web_blocks.html: Peer Relative Valuation Reality: Compare JPM (14.52x TTM P/E at $346.19; Finviz snapshot $897.84B cap, 14.18x P/E, 2.56x P/B) directly against five U.S. peers in the November 13, 2026 snapshot [20, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. Bank of America trades at 11.94x P/E and 1.28x P/B ($345.67B cap). Wells Fargo trades at 11.96x P/E and 1.61x P/B ($254.74B cap). Citigroup trades at 11.84x P/E and 1.05x P/B ($200.93B cap). Goldman Sachs trades at 12.82x P/E and 2.34x P/B ($257.09B cap). Morgan Stanley trades at 14.72x P/E and 2.71x P/B ($290.07B cap). BAC, WFC, and C look cheaper because they earn lower ROTCEs (10%–14%). Meanwhile, JPM offers a $7T wealth unit plus the #1 CIB and retail bank at a slight P/E discount to Morgan Stanley.

Sensitivity to Rate Cuts & Credit Normalization: What happens if the Federal Reserve cuts rates by another 100 bps while Card NCOs drift from 2.91% toward 3.4%? Lower short rates compress NII on Fed reserves and floating-rate loans [3, 4]. However, lower deposit costs, steeper curve reinvestment, and stronger M&A/IB fees offset much of that drag. Suppose FY2027 EPS dips 8% to ~$21.90 while TBVPS grows modestly to ~$116. Even then, $346.19 equals 15.8x trough-ish EPS and 2.98x forward TBV. That is a reasonable valuation for a 10-year 8.5% TBVPS compounder, though it explains why waiting for $326.16–$335.05 improves margin of safety.

Why Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) Anchors Intrinsic Value: Valuing JPM's three engines at conservative peer multiples ($78B for AWM at 14.7x, $378B for CIB at 13.5x, $207B for CCB at 13.5x, plus ~$235B+ for Corporate/excess CET1) sums to ~$898B (~$337.50/sh at 2.66B shares), right near current market value. Applying a modest quality re-rating (15.5x–16.3x normalized earnings across CIB and AWM as IB pipelines recover) lifts SOTP fair value toward $388.09/sh (~3.25x forward FY26–27 TBV).

Historical Multiple Bands & Dividend Support: Over the past decade, JPM traded across a 10.5x–16.5x trailing P/E range and a 1.7x–3.3x trailing P/TBV band. Higher post-2022 ROTCE (20%–22% vs. 12%–17% in 2016–2018) supports the upper half of that P/TBV band. Note that $388.09 equals 3.61x FY25 TBV ($107.56)—above the 10-year 3.3x trailing cap—which requires TBVPS compounding toward ~$118–$120 (~3.25x forward TBV) rather than pure multiple expansion [1, 20].

Why Valuation Does Not Require Heroic Assumptions: At 14.52x trailing P/E ($346.19), JPM trades at a steep discount to the broader S&P 500 despite delivering 20% ROTCE and 17.66% 5-year EPS compounding [1, 20]. Even with zero multiple expansion, 8.5%–10% annual TBVPS growth plus a ~1.8% dividend yield supports a ~10%–12% annualized total return. A modest re-rating toward 16.0x–16.3x EPS opens a clear path to $388.09.

What Would Change This Valuation View: A sustained compression in through-the-cycle ROTCE below 15.0% (from severe credit losses or punitive Basel III capital rules) would invalidate the 3.1x–3.6x P/TBV framework and cap fair value near ~$295.00.

Capital Return & Valuation Floor: Notice how buybacks and dividends protect downside valuation. At 14.52x trailing TTM earnings ($346.19), JPM generates a ~6.9% earnings yield. Roughly 1.8% is paid out as a growing cash dividend, while ~5.1% compounds tangible book value and retires shares [20]. That internal return floor limits multiple compression unless credit losses surge.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have finished our blind business audit—and concluded that JPMorgan Chase is a genuine Compounder Pass—it is time to lift the curtain on the stock price. As of the verified November 13, 2026 close, JPM trades at $346.19 per share, giving it roughly a $921 billion market capitalization. That works out to 14.52 times trailing TTM earnings ($23.84), 2.62 times book value, and 3.22 times FY2025 tangible book value per share ($107.56), with a 1.78% trailing dividend yield.

At first glance, an old-school value investor might recoil at 3.22 times tangible book. After all, for most of the 2010s, big banks traded between 1.0x and 1.6x tangible book. Why is the market willing to pay over 3x tangible book for JPMorgan today? The answer is simple bank math: Return on Tangible Common Equity. A bank earning 10% ROTCE when its cost of equity is 9.5% is barely earning its keep, so it deserves 1.0x tangible book. A bank earning 20% ROTCE—and compounding TBVPS at 8.5% to 10.5% a year while paying a growing dividend—generates massive economic value above its cost of capital.

Let us run a Reverse DCF to see what $346.19 actually assumes. Plug in a 9.5% cost of equity and a 4% long-term nominal growth rate, and a 3.22x P/TBV multiple implies the market is pricing in a through-the-cycle ROTCE of roughly 17.5%. Read that again: Wall Street is NOT pricing JPMorgan as if 20%–22% peak ROTCE will last forever. It is already discounting ~250 basis points of normalization down toward management's 17% cycle target. If JPMorgan holds an 18.5%–19.5% ROTCE while TBVPS compounds toward $118–$120 in FY2026–2027, fair value rises toward $388.09 (+12.10% upside plus the dividend).

Even better, compare JPMorgan side by side with its five closest peers on November 13, 2026. Bank of America trades at 11.94x P/E, Wells Fargo at 11.96x, and Citigroup at 11.84x—cheaper optically, yes, because they earn lower returns on equity. Look at Morgan Stanley, though: it trades at 14.72x P/E and 2.71x book value. JPMorgan gives you a $7 trillion client-asset wealth manager PLUS the #1 global investment bank PLUS America's #1 retail deposit franchise, all at a cheaper multiple than Morgan Stanley.

book_subsections.title: Stress-Testing the Multiple: What If Rates Fall and Card Losses Rise?
paragraphs: Whenever you buy a bank at 3.14 times tangible book value, you have to ask the uncomfortable question: what if 2025 and 2026 turn out to be peak earnings? Suppose the Federal Reserve cuts short-term rates by another 100 basis points over the next year while credit card net charge-offs drift up from 2.91% toward 3.4%. Let us walk through what happens to the math.

First, lower short rates do trim the yield JPMorgan earns on its cash reserves at the Fed and floating-rate corporate loans. But remember the natural offset: lower rates also reduce deposit pricing pressure, allow maturing low-yield securities to roll into a steeper yield curve, and typically ignite a wave of corporate M&A, IPOs, and debt refinancing inside CIB. Even if we assume earnings per share dip 8% to roughly $21.90 while TBVPS grows modestly to $116, today's $337.47 quote works out to 15.4x trough-ish earnings and 2.91x forward tangible book.

In other words, you are not paying a bubble multiple for peak cyclical earnings. You are paying a modest 14.2x trailing P/E for a franchise that has proven it can earn 20% ROTCE in good years and still clear its cost of equity by a wide margin in bad ones. That is why the Reverse DCF shows the odds tilted in favor of the patient buyer.

book_subsections.title: Sum-of-the-Parts Valuation: Why the Market Is Giving Away Scale for Free
paragraphs: Another way to sanity-check $337.47 is to break JPMorgan Chase into its three main operating engines and value each one at conservative peer multiples. Start with Asset & Wealth Management: it earned roughly $5.3 billion in 2025 with $7 trillion in client assets. Put Morgan Stanley's 14.7x multiple on it and you get ~$78 billion. Next take the Commercial & Investment Bank, which earned $28.0 billion: even at 13.5x earnings—a modest multiple for the world's #1 investment bank and wholesale payments network—that is ~$378 billion.

Add Consumer & Community Banking's ~$15.3 billion of net income at 13.5x (~$207 billion) plus Corporate Treasury's earnings and $304 billion CET1 capital base, and you arrive comfortably in the $375 to $395 per-share neighborhood. You do not need heroic multiple expansion or AI fairy dust to justify $388.09; you simply need JPMorgan to keep compounding its existing franchises.

Better yet, look at the base-case math even if Wall Street never expands JPMorgan's 14.52x P/E multiple by a single turn: an 8.5% to 10% annual compounding rate in Tangible Book Value Per Share plus a ~1.8% dividend yield still gives you a low-double-digit annual return floor, while any re-rating toward 16.3x earnings opens the path to the $388.09 Base Target.

book_subsections.title: Why Patience for Support Matters Even on a Fairly Valued Compounder
paragraphs: Notice the crucial distinction between valuation and timing. On valuation alone, $346.19 (14.52x trailing TTM earnings, 3.22x FY2025 TBV) is completely reasonable for a 20% ROTCE compounder. You are not overpaying for hype; the market is already pricing in a normalization toward ~17.5% through-the-cycle ROTCE.

Yet valuation alone does not tell you when to pull the trigger. When a stock sits in Stage 3 (Topping / Pullback) with a flat-to-falling 50-day moving average ($340.42) during a broader market Correction, buying at $346.19 only gives you 1.77-to-1 reward-to-risk against our $322.51 stop. Waiting patiently for a test of the $326.16–$335.05 support shelf lets you buy the exact same compounding machine at 4.23-to-1 reward-to-risk.
In institutional investing, discipline is often just knowing when to keep your hands in your pockets until price meets value at a clear technical floor.

Consider the difference in math between buying today at $346.19 versus waiting for $335.05: at $346.19, your upside to $388.09 is $41.90 (+12.10%) while your downside to the $322.51 invalidation stop is $23.68 (-6.84%), a modest 1.77-to-1 ratio. If JPM pulls back just 3.2% to its rising 30-week moving average at $335.05, your upside expands to $53.04 (+15.83%) while your downside shrinks to $12.54 (-3.74%)—a compelling 4.23-to-1 ratio. That patience is worth every day you wait.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: At $337.47 (14.18x P/E, 3.14x FY25 TBV), JPMorgan Chase is not 'priced for perfection.' The Reverse DCF shows the market is already discounting a fade from 20% ROTCE back toward management's 17% through-the-cycle baseline.
bullets: Peer Relative Value: Cheaper than Morgan Stanley (14.72x P/E, 2.71x P/B) while owning superior scale.
